nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-01.title: Count per hour
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-01.body:
Reading a time like 3:24 as the number $324$, divisibility by $4$ depends only on the last two digits, i.e. the minutes. In every hour the minutes $00,04,08,\dots,56$ work: $\frac{60}{4}=15$ times. Over $12$ hours that is $12\cdot15=180$.

**Answer: 180**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-01.title: Check the hour digits don't matter
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-01.body:
A time $H{:}MM$ is the number $100H+MM$. Since $100$ is divisible by $4$, the number is a multiple of $4$ exactly when $MM$ is. Each of the $12$ hours (12, 1, 2, …, 11) contributes the $15$ multiples of 4 from $00$ to $56$, giving $180$.

**Answer: 180**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-02.title: AF bisects angle DAE
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-02.body:
Since $\angle DAB=90^\circ$ and $\angle FAB=60^\circ$, $\angle DAF=30^\circ$, while $\angle DAE=60^\circ$. So ray $AF$ bisects $\angle DAE$; let it meet $DE$ at $G$. The overlap is $\triangle AGE$ (the part of $\triangle ADE$ on the $B$ side of $AF$; $\triangle ABF$ is large enough to contain it). In the equilateral triangle $ADE$ the angle bisector $AG$ is also a median, so it halves the area:
$$[AGE]=\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot4^2=2\sqrt3.$$

**Answer: $2\sqrt3$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-02.title: Coordinates
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-02.body:
Let $D=(0,0)$, $A=(0,4)$, $B=(7,4)$. Then $E=(2\sqrt3,2)$ and line $AF$ goes down from $A$ at $60^\circ$ below $AB$: points $(t,4-\sqrt3t)$. It meets $DE$ (the line $y=x/\sqrt3$) at $G=(\sqrt3,1)$, the midpoint of $DE$. Triangle $AGE$ has vertices $(0,4),(\sqrt3,1),(2\sqrt3,2)$; by the shoelace formula its area is $\frac12|0(1-2)+\sqrt3(2-4)+2\sqrt3(4-1)|=\frac12\cdot4\sqrt3=2\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt3$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-03.title: Isosceles triangle
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-03.body:
By the Pythagorean theorem, $CD=DB=\sqrt{16+9}=5$ and $BC=\sqrt{16+16}=4\sqrt2$. In isosceles $\triangle BCD$, the altitude from $D$ hits the midpoint $E$ of $BC$, so $EB=2\sqrt2$ and $DE=\sqrt{25-8}=\sqrt{17}$. The area is $\frac12\cdot4\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt{17}=2\sqrt{34}$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{34}$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-03.title: Pythagorean theorem for areas
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-03.body:
For a right-corner tetrahedron, the square of the area of the face opposite the right corner equals the sum of the squares of the other three face areas: $[ABC]=8$, $[ABD]=[ACD]=6$. So $[BCD]^2=64+36+36=136$ and $[BCD]=\sqrt{136}=2\sqrt{34}$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{34}$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-04.title: Symmetry before the last coin
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-04.body:
Compare after Dave's first 3 coins. Let $p$ be the probability Carrie is ahead; by symmetry Dave is ahead with probability $p$, and they tie with probability $1-2p$. If Carrie is ahead, Dave's 4th coin cannot overtake her (it only brings a tie at most, and a tie still counts); if tied, Carrie needs Dave's 4th coin to be tails (probability $\frac12$); if Dave is ahead, Carrie loses. Total: $p+\frac12(1-2p)=\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-04.title: Direct count
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-04.body:
Carrie's heads $C$ has distribution $1,3,3,1$ (out of 8) for $0..3$; Dave's $D$ has $1,4,6,4,1$ (out of 16) for $0..4$. Favorable pairs with $C\ge D$: $C=0$: $1\cdot1$; $C=1$: $3\cdot5$; $C=2$: $3\cdot11$; $C=3$: $1\cdot15$. Total $1+15+33+15=64$ out of $128$, i.e. $\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-06.title: Integer and fractional parts
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-06.body:
Write $x=I+F$ with $I=\lfloor x\rfloor$, $0\le F<1$. Expanding $(x-I)^2=x^2-2xI+I^2$, the equation becomes $2xI=\lfloor x^2\rfloor+I^2$. Since $x^2=I^2+2IF+F^2$, $\lfloor x^2\rfloor=I^2+\lfloor 2IF+F^2\rfloor$, and the equation reduces to
$$2IF=\lfloor 2IF+F^2\rfloor.$$
If $2IF$ is an integer, this holds because $0\le F^2<1$; conversely the right side is an integer, so $2IF$ must be. Hence the solutions are exactly $x=I+\frac{k}{2I}$ with $k=0,1,\dots,2I-1$, giving $2I$ solutions for each $I$. For $I=1,\dots,6$ the total is $2+4+6+8+10+12=42$.

**Answer: 42**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-06.title: Graphical view
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-06.body:
On each interval $[k,k+1)$, the right side $(x-k)^2$ rises from $0$ to $1$ once, while $x^2-\lfloor x^2\rfloor$ rises from $0$ to $1$ once for each unit increase of $x^2$, i.e. $(k+1)^2-k^2=2k+1$ times. The single slow parabola crosses the $2k+1$ fast sawtooth teeth once on each of the first $2k$ teeth (including the start point $x=k$) and never on the last (they would only meet at the excluded endpoint). So there are $2k$ solutions in $[k,k+1)$, and $\sum_{k=1}^{6}2k=42$.

**Answer: 42**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-07.title: Common denominator
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-07.body:
Let $a=\sqrt7+\sqrt5$ and $b=\sqrt7-\sqrt5$. Then $ab=7-5=2$ and $a^2+b^2=(12+2\sqrt{35})+(12-2\sqrt{35})=24$, so
$$\frac ab+\frac ba=\frac{a^2+b^2}{ab}=\frac{24}{2}=12.$$

**Answer: 12**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-08.title: Smallest digit sum 27
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-08.body:
$s(N)$ must be a positive multiple of 27, so at least 27. A number with at most 3 digits has $s(N)\le27$ with equality only for $999=27\cdot37$, which is divisible by 27. So $N$ has at least 4 digits. The smallest 4-digit numbers with digit sum 27 start with $1$, followed by digits summing to $26$: an $8$ and two $9$s, the smallest being $1899$. Since $1899=27\cdot70+9$, it is not divisible by 27.

**Answer: 1899**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-08.title: Check candidates in order
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-08.body:
Four-digit numbers with digit sum 27 in increasing order: $1899, 1989, 1998, 2799,\dots$. The first, $1899$, already works: $1899/27=70\tfrac13$. And every smaller positive integer has digit sum below 27 except $999$, which is a multiple of 27.

**Answer: 1899**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-09.title: Different colors
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-09.body:
The probability of different colors must also be $\frac12$: $\frac{3k}{\binom{k+3}{2}}=\frac12$. So $12k=(k+3)(k+2)=k^2+5k+6$, i.e. $k^2-7k+6=(k-1)(k-6)=0$. Thus $k=1$ or $k=6$.

**Answer: $k=1, 6$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-09.title: Check
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-09.body:
$k=1$: pairs from 4 socks: 6 total, same color $\binom32=3$, probability $\frac12$. $k=6$: 36 pairs, same color $\binom32+\binom62=3+15=18$, probability $\frac12$. Both work.

**Answer: $k=1, 6$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-10.title: Difference of squares
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-10.body:
Let $n=k^2$ and $n+45=a^2$ with positive integers $a>k$. Then $(a+k)(a-k)=45$, so $(a+k,a-k)\in\{(45,1),(15,3),(9,5)\}$, giving $k=22,6,2$ and $n=484,36,4$. Their sum is $524$.

**Answer: 524**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-10.title: Consecutive odd numbers
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-10.body:
$a^2-k^2=45$ means $45$ is a sum of the consecutive odd numbers $2k+1,\dots,2a-1$. The factor pairs of 45 give exactly three such representations ($45$; $13+15+17$; $5+7+9+11+13$), i.e. $k=22,6,2$. Sum of $n=k^2$: $484+36+4=524$.

**Answer: 524**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-11.title: Use the equation
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-11.body:
Since $p^2-3p+3=0$ and $q^2-3q+3=0$, we have $p^2-3p+5=2$ and $q^2-3q+6=3$. The product is $6$.

**Answer: 6**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-11.title: Substitute
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-11.body:
$p^2-3p=-3$ and $q^2-3q=-3$ for both roots, regardless of which is which, so the product is $(-3+5)(-3+6)=6$.

**Answer: 6**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-12.title: Angle bisector and similar triangles
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-12.body:
Inscribed angles give $\angle BDA=\angle BCA=60^\circ$ and $\angle ADC=\angle ABC=60^\circ$, so $DE$ bisects $\angle BDC=120^\circ$. By the Law of Cosines, $BC^2=14^2+35^2+14\cdot35=1911=49\cdot39$. By the angle bisector theorem $BE:EC=14:35=2:5$; write $BE=2x$, $EC=5x$, so $49x^2=49\cdot39$ and $x^2=39$.

In $\triangle BDE$ (angle $60^\circ$ at $D$): $BE^2=BD^2+DE^2-BD\cdot DE$, i.e. $156=196+DE^2-14DE$, so $DE^2-14DE+40=0$ and $DE\in\{4,10\}$. In $\triangle CDE$: $975=1225+DE^2-35DE$, so $DE^2-35DE+250=0$ and $DE\in\{10,25\}$. Both hold only for $DE=10$.

**Answer: 10**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-12.title: Area of the bisected angle
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-12.body:
Split $\triangle BDC$ along the bisector $DE$ into two triangles with $60^\circ$ angles at $D$:
$$\tfrac12\cdot14\cdot35\sin120^\circ=\tfrac12\cdot14\cdot DE\sin60^\circ+\tfrac12\cdot35\cdot DE\sin60^\circ.$$
Since $\sin120^\circ=\sin60^\circ$, this gives $490=49\,DE$, so $DE=10$ (equivalently $\frac1{DE}=\frac1{14}+\frac1{35}$).

**Answer: 10**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-13.title: Both terms vanish
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-13.body:
A sum of absolute values is zero only if each is zero: $3x+y=12$ and $x+3y=-4$. Adding gives $4x+4y=8$, so $x+y=2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-13.title: Solve the system
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-13.body:
From $3x+y=12$ and $x+3y=-4$: multiply the first by 3 and subtract: $8x=40$, $x=5$, $y=-3$. So $x+y=2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-14.title: Discriminants mod 4
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-14.body:
For $ax^2+bx+c$ with integers, $D=b^2-4ac\equiv b^2\equiv0$ or $1\pmod4$. Irrational roots need $D$ to be a positive non-square. Candidates above 24: $25$ is a perfect square (rational roots), $26$ and $27$ are $\equiv2,3\pmod4$ and impossible, and $28$ works, e.g. $x^2+6x+2$ has $D=36-8=28$.

**Answer: 28**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-14.title: Example and minimality
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-14.body:
$x^2+6x+2=0$ has roots $-3\pm\sqrt7$, irrational, with $D=28$. A smaller $D>24$ would be $25$, $26$ or $27$; $25$ gives rational roots and $26,27$ cannot equal $b^2-4ac$ since $b^2\bmod4\in\{0,1\}$.

**Answer: 28**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-15.title: Squares have an odd number of divisors
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-15.body:
If $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_k^{e_k}$, the number of divisors is $(e_1+1)\cdots(e_k+1)$, which is odd exactly when every $e_i$ is even, i.e. when $n$ is a perfect square. So we sum all $n\le100$ except the squares: $5050-(1^2+\cdots+10^2)=5050-385=4665$.

**Answer: 4665**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-15.title: Pairing divisors
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-15.body:
Divisors of $n$ pair up as $d\leftrightarrow n/d$; the only unpaired divisor is $\sqrt n$ when $n$ is a square. So non-squares have an even number of divisors. Sum of $1..100$ is $5050$; the squares sum to $\frac{10\cdot11\cdot21}{6}=385$; the answer is $4665$.

**Answer: 4665**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-16.title: Two formulas for the area
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-16.body:
Let $BD=8y$ and $AC=6y$. The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so the side is $\sqrt{(4y)^2+(3y)^2}=5y$. The area is $\frac12\cdot8y\cdot6y=24y^2$, and also side $\times$ height $=5y\cdot15=75y$. So $24y^2=75y$, $y=\frac{25}{8}$, and $BD=8y=25$.

**Answer: 25**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-16.title: Trigonometry
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-16.body:
Half-diagonals $4y,3y$ give $\tan\frac{\angle B}{2}=\frac{3}{4}$ (half of $AC$ over half of $BD$), so $\sin\angle B=\frac{2\cdot\frac34}{1+\frac9{16}}=\frac{24}{25}$. The height from $D$ to $BC$ equals $DC\sin\angle C=s\sin\angle B$, so $s=15\cdot\frac{25}{24}=\frac{125}{8}$. Then $BD=\frac85s=25$.

**Answer: 25**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-17.title: Factor
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-17.body:
$a+b>ab\iff ab-a-b+1<1\iff(a-1)(b-1)<1$. Both factors are nonnegative integers, so their product is $0$: $a=1$ or $b=1$. That is $5+5-1=9$ of the $25$ pairs, probability $\frac9{25}$.

**Answer: $\frac9{25}$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-17.title: Check cases
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-17.body:
If $a,b\ge2$ then $ab\ge2\max(a,b)\ge a+b$, so the inequality fails. If $a=1$, it reads $1+b>b$, always true; likewise for $b=1$. So exactly the $9$ pairs with a $1$ work: $\frac{9}{25}$.

**Answer: $\frac9{25}$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-18.title: Distances in the plane
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-18.body:
$f(x)=\sqrt{(x-2)^2+3^2}+\sqrt{(x+1)^2+(-2)^2}$ is $AP+BP$ for $P=(x,0)$, $A=(2,3)$, $B=(-1,-2)$. By the triangle inequality $AP+BP\ge AB=\sqrt{3^2+5^2}=\sqrt{34}$, with equality when $P$ lies on segment $AB$. Since $A$ and $B$ are on opposite sides of the $x$-axis, segment $AB$ crosses it, at $x=\frac15$ (line $3y=5x-1$). So the minimum is $\sqrt{34}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{34}$**

nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-18.title: Minkowski inequality
nyciml-2019-20-fall-junior-18.body:
$\sqrt{u_1^2+v_1^2}+\sqrt{u_2^2+v_2^2}\ge\sqrt{(u_1+u_2)^2+(v_1+v_2)^2}$. With $(u_1,v_1)=(2-x,3)$ and $(u_2,v_2)=(x+1,2)$, the right side is $\sqrt{3^2+5^2}=\sqrt{34}$, attained when the vectors are parallel: $\frac{2-x}{3}=\frac{x+1}{2}$, i.e. $x=\frac15$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{34}$**
